title: Learn AI

mentor.name: ECHO-2
mentor.character: Answers your questions with better questions.

summary: No code needed. Learn what AI assistants really are, how to talk to them, how to write great prompts, check their answers and stay safe, then use skills, tools and AI agents like a pro.

chapters.title: What AI Is, and What It Is Not

lessons.title: A machine that predicts words
lessons.goal: You can say in one sentence what an AI assistant actually does when it answers you.
lessons.theory:
An AI assistant such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini is built on a **language model**. A language model is a computer program trained on a huge amount of text: books, websites, articles and much more.

During training it did one job over and over: look at some text and **predict the next word**. After billions of examples it became very good at it. Along the way it picked up grammar, facts, styles of writing and the way explanations usually go.

When you send a message, the assistant writes its reply one small piece at a time. Each time, it picks a likely next word based on your message and everything written so far. (Strictly, it works with pieces of words called **tokens**, but "words" is close enough.)

After that first training, the model gets extra training to follow instructions and act as a helpful, polite assistant. That is why it answers your question instead of just continuing your sentence.

This one idea explains a lot:

- It can write smoothly about almost any topic, because it has seen so much text.
- It does not look answers up in a list of facts. It builds each answer from patterns.
- It can write something that sounds right but is not, because sounding right is what it learned best.

Keep this picture in mind. Every other mission in this course builds on it.
lessons.task: Which sentence best describes what an AI assistant does when it answers you?
lessons.hint: Think about the one job the model practised again and again during its training.

options: It looks up your question in a giant database of correct answers and copies the matching one.
It writes the answer one piece at a time, each time predicting a likely next word from patterns it learned in training.
It thinks about your question the way a person does, using its own memories and feelings.
It passes your question to a team of experts who type the reply very quickly.
why: There is no database of correct answers. The model builds each answer from patterns it learned, which is also why it can be wrong.
Right. It predicts a likely next word again and again, using your message and what it has written so far.
It is a program, not a person. It has no life of its own to remember and no feelings, even when it sounds friendly.
No people write the replies. The whole answer comes from the model, which is why it arrives in seconds.
check.explain: An AI assistant is a language model that writes its reply piece by piece, predicting a likely next word each time. It learned those patterns from huge amounts of text.

lessons.title: Not a search engine, not a person
lessons.goal: You can explain how an AI assistant differs from a search engine and from a person, and what that means for trusting its answers.
lessons.theory:
Because an AI assistant answers questions, it is easy to treat it like a search engine or like a very clever friend. It is neither, and knowing the difference helps you use it well.

**A search engine** finds pages that already exist and shows you links. You read the sources yourself and decide what to trust.

**An AI assistant** writes a brand-new answer. It does not point to one page; it combines patterns from everything it learned. That makes it great for explaining, summarising and brainstorming. But on its own, it does not tell you where a fact came from.

Many assistants can now also search the web as a tool. When they do, they read some pages and then write a summary, often with links. That helps, but the summary is still written by the model, so it can still misread or mix things up. Open the links for anything important.

**It is not a person either.** It can sound warm, patient and funny, because it learned from text written by people. But it does not know you the way a friend does, and its opinions are not a friend's advice. It can also agree with you too easily, just to be helpful.

A good way to think of it: a very well-read helper that can explain almost anything, and whose answers you still double-check.
lessons.task: Maya asks an AI assistant "When did the Eiffel Tower open?" and gets a confident answer with no link. What is the best way to think about that answer?
lessons.hint: Remember what a search engine gives you and what an assistant gives you.

options: It is copied from the best web page on the topic, so it is exactly as reliable as that page.
It is the assistant's personal opinion, so she should ask again to see if it changes its mind.
It is new text the model wrote from patterns it learned. A famous fact is probably right, but for anything important she should check a reliable source.
It must be wrong, because AI assistants cannot know any facts.
why: Without a search, the assistant does not copy a page. It writes new text from patterns, and no source is attached to it.
A date is not an opinion. Asking again may give the same answer or a different one, and neither proves it is right. Only an outside source can.
Right. The model wrote that sentence itself, so there is no source behind it. Well-known facts are usually right, but check what matters.
Too far. Assistants get many well-known facts right. The point is that they can also be wrong, so you check what matters.
check.explain: The assistant wrote that answer itself from learned patterns. Famous facts are usually right, but no source comes with it, so check anything that matters.

lessons.title: Sounding sure is not being right
lessons.goal: You can explain what a hallucination is, where it is most likely, and what to do about it.
lessons.theory:
Sometimes an AI assistant states something false as if it were a plain fact. This is called a **hallucination**. The word sounds dramatic, but the cause is simple: the model predicts text that fits, and a made-up detail can fit perfectly well.

Hallucinations are most common when:

- you ask for exact details: dates, numbers, names, quotes
- you ask for sources: it may invent a book, an article or a web link that does not exist
- the topic is rare, very local or very new, so it saw little text about it
- your question assumes something false, like "Why did Einstein win two Nobel Prizes?" (he won one)

The tricky part is the tone. A made-up answer usually sounds just as calm and confident as a correct one. The assistant is not lying on purpose. It simply cannot always tell when it is guessing.

So how sure it sounds tells you nothing about whether it is right. What helps:

- For anything important, check a reliable source: your textbook, your teacher, an official website.
- Be extra careful with quotes, statistics and references.
- If you suspect a mistake, say so and ask it to double-check. It may correct itself, but check the correction too.

Later in this course you will learn a full routine for checking answers.
lessons.task: You ask an assistant for three books about the history of chess for a school project. It gives three titles with authors, and they all sound real. What should you do?
lessons.hint: Which option checks the books somewhere outside the chat?

options: Look up each title in a library catalogue or a bookshop website before you use it, because assistants can invent books that sound real.
Use them as they are. The assistant sounded completely sure, so they must exist.
Ask the assistant "Are you sure?" and trust the titles if it says yes.
Throw the whole list away. Anything an AI says about books is always made up.
why: Right. Sources are a classic place for hallucinations, and a quick outside check tells you which books are real.
Confidence is not evidence. A made-up book sounds exactly as sure as a real one.
Asking can help it catch a mistake, but its "yes" is also predicted text. Only an outside source can confirm the books exist.
Too far. Many of its suggestions will be real and useful. You just check them before you rely on them.
check.explain: Assistants can invent sources that sound real, and a made-up title sounds just as confident as a real one. Checking outside the chat is the only way to be sure.

lessons.title: Frozen in time
lessons.goal: You can explain why an assistant may not know about recent events, and what to do when you need something current.
lessons.theory:
A language model learns from text collected up to a certain date. That date is called its **training cutoff**, or knowledge cutoff. Anything that happened later was never in its training text, so the model has simply not seen it.

This matters more than you might think. The model may not know:

- recent news, sports results or election results
- the newest phone, game or app update
- a change at your school or in an exam this year
- today's price of anything

Worse, it may not realise what it is missing. Ask about a recent event and it might describe an older one, or guess, in the same confident tone.

Some assistants can **search the web** and will do so for questions about recent things. When an answer comes with links to fresh pages, that is usually a sign it searched. Without a search, you only get what the model learned before its cutoff.

Good habits:

- For anything recent, use an assistant that searches, or check a news site or official page yourself.
- You can ask "How recent is your information on this?" Treat the reply as a hint, not a promise.
- When the latest facts matter, put them in your message yourself.

The model's knowledge is a snapshot. It is huge, but it is not live.
lessons.task: You want to know who won last weekend's football final. The assistant answers instantly, with no links, and names a team. What is the most likely problem?
lessons.hint: Think about when the model's training text was collected, and what "no links" suggests.

options: Football is too complicated for AI assistants to understand.
The assistant is hiding the real result on purpose.
There is no problem: assistants always know the latest results.
The final probably happened after its training cutoff, so without a web search it may be guessing or describing an older final.
why: The topic is not the issue. An assistant can explain football rules very well. The problem is how recent the event is.
It is not hiding anything. It simply never saw text about an event after its training cutoff.
Models learn from text up to a cutoff date. Without a web search they cannot know what happened last weekend.
Right. Last weekend is almost certainly after its training cutoff, and no links suggests it did not search.
check.explain: The model only knows what was in its training text, which stops at a cutoff date. For last weekend's result you need a web search or a news site.

lessons.title: Many kinds of AI tools
lessons.goal: You can name the main kinds of AI tools and pick the right one for a job.
lessons.theory:
"AI" is not one single app. These are the main kinds of AI tools you will meet:

- **Chat assistants** such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini. You type or speak, and they answer in text. They explain, summarise, brainstorm, translate and help you plan.
- **Image generators** create a picture from a written description, or change an existing picture.
- **Voice tools** turn speech into text, read text aloud, or let you have a spoken conversation with an assistant.
- **Coding helpers** suggest and explain computer code for people who program.
- **AI agents** do more than answer: they take steps to finish a task, like searching several websites, filling in a form or organising files, checking with you along the way.

The lines are blurring. Many chat assistants can now also look at a photo you upload, talk out loud, search the web or make images. Still, the core idea is the same: these tools learned from huge amounts of data, and they all make mistakes sometimes.

Picking the right kind of tool saves time. If you want a picture, an image tool will do better than a description. If you want something explained, a chat assistant is the place to start. And if you want a task done step by step, that is the job of an agent, which you will meet later in this course.
lessons.task: Which pairing of a job and an AI tool fits best?
lessons.hint: For each option, ask yourself what that kind of tool actually produces.

options: Making a poster picture of a dragon reading a book: a **coding helper**
Getting photosynthesis explained in simple words, then asking follow-up questions: a **chat assistant**
Turning a recorded interview into written text: an **image generator**
Checking several websites and filling in a form, step by step: a **voice tool** that reads text aloud
why: A coding helper suggests computer code. Making a picture from a description is the job of an image generator.
Right. Explaining a topic and answering follow-up questions is exactly what chat assistants are built for.
Image generators make pictures. Turning speech into text is a job for a voice tool.
Reading text aloud does not take steps for you. Doing a task across several websites is what an AI agent is for.
check.explain: Explaining a topic and answering follow-up questions is exactly what chat assistants are built for.

lessons.title: Great at, bad at
lessons.goal: You can tell a good job for an AI assistant from a risky one, and plan to use it as a tutor rather than a shortcut.
lessons.theory:
Now that you know how an AI assistant works, you can predict where it shines and where it stumbles.

**Great at:**

- explaining a topic in different ways until it clicks
- giving examples, comparisons and practice questions
- brainstorming ideas for a project, a story or a hobby
- summarising long text you give it, and tidying up notes
- giving feedback on your writing: clarity, structure, spelling
- translating and rephrasing

**Weak or risky:**

- exact facts, dates, quotes and sources, if you do not check them
- very recent events, unless it searches the web
- exact counting and long calculations (it can slip, so check the numbers)
- knowing you: it only knows what you tell it
- questions where you need a trusted adult or expert, like health, safety or legal problems

It also matters **how** you use it. Using AI to learn means it explains, asks you questions and gives feedback, while you do the thinking. Handing in its work as your own skips the learning, and most schools treat it as cheating. The best students use it like a patient tutor who is always available.

A simple rule: let AI help you understand, practise and improve. Then check the facts and make the final work your own.
lessons.task: You have a history test on the Roman Empire next week. Which plan uses an AI assistant best?
lessons.hint: Look for the plan that uses its strengths and protects you from its weaknesses.

options: Ask it to write answers to last year's test and memorise them word for word.
Ask it for all the dates you need and copy them into your notes without checking, since dates are easy for it.
Ask it to explain the parts you find confusing and to quiz you, then check key dates and names in your textbook.
Avoid it completely, because AI tools are useless for studying.
why: Memorising its text skips the understanding a test checks, and you might learn its mistakes by heart.
Exact dates are one of the places it can slip. Anything you put in your notes for a test is worth checking.
Right. Explaining and quizzing are its strengths, and checking dates and names covers its weak spot.
Too far. Explaining and quizzing are exactly what it is great at. You just check the facts.
check.explain: Explaining and quizzing are exactly what assistants do well, and checking key facts in your textbook protects you from their mistakes. You still do the learning.

lessons.title: Ask one clear thing
lessons.goal: You can write a first message that asks one clear thing about a specific topic.
lessons.theory:
The fastest way to a good answer is a clear question. The assistant cannot see inside your head. It only has the words you type.

A clear message usually has three things:

- **One main request.** Ask for one thing at a time. "Explain photosynthesis, write a poem about it and plan my week" gets you three rushed answers.
- **A specific topic.** "Tell me about space" could mean anything. "How do black holes form?" points somewhere.
- **What you want back.** An explanation? A list? Three ideas? A short summary? Say so.

Compare these two messages:

```text
help with science
```

```text
Can you explain how vaccines train the immune system? Keep it short.
```

The first one forces the assistant to guess. It might ask what you mean, or write a long general answer you did not need. The second gives the topic, the request and even the length.

You do not need special words or a secret formula. Write the way you would ask a helpful teacher: plainly, in full sentences, with enough detail that someone who does not know you would still understand.

Got several questions? That is fine. Ask them one after another in the same chat.
lessons.task: Which message is most likely to get a useful answer on the first try?
lessons.hint: Look for one request, a specific topic, and a clue about what the answer should look like.

options: science stuff pls
Tell me everything about history, maths and also how to draw hands.
What is it and why does it happen?
Can you explain why the Moon has phases, in a few short paragraphs?
why: It has no specific topic and no clear request, so the assistant has to guess what you want.
Three big unrelated topics in one message. Ask one thing at a time and each answer gets better.
"It" could be anything. In a new chat the assistant has no idea what you mean, so name the topic.
Right. One request, a specific topic, and a hint about the length of the answer.
check.explain: It asks one thing, names a specific topic and says what kind of answer you want.

lessons.title: Follow-ups keep the context
lessons.goal: You can use follow-up questions that build on the conversation instead of starting over.
lessons.theory:
A conversation with an AI assistant is not a string of separate questions. Inside one chat, the assistant sees the whole conversation so far every time it answers. This is called the **context**.

So you can build on what came before:

```text
You: How do bees make honey?
AI: (explains nectar, enzymes and evaporation)
You: Why do they fan their wings for that part?
```

"That part" works because the assistant can see its own explanation above. You do not need to repeat everything.

Useful follow-ups:

- "Can you give me an example of that?"
- "What does the word 'enzyme' mean?"
- "How is that different from how wasps live?"
- "Go back to your second point and explain it more."

Follow-ups are where the real learning happens. The first answer gives you the outline, and your questions dig into the parts you did not get.

Two things to remember. The context only lasts **within that chat**: a new chat starts with an empty page, unless your assistant has a separate memory feature switched on. And in very long chats, the assistant can lose track of details from early on, so repeat anything important.
lessons.task: Earlier in the same chat, the assistant explained how volcanoes erupt. Now you type: "Can you give me a real example of that?" What happens?
lessons.hint: What can the assistant see each time it writes a reply in the same chat?

options: It understands that "that" means a volcanic eruption, because it can see the earlier conversation in this chat.
It gets confused, because every message is treated as a brand-new question.
It can answer, but only if you open a new chat first.
It cannot answer until you repeat the whole first question word for word.
why: Right. The whole chat so far is its context, so "that" clearly points to the eruption it just explained.
Inside one chat, the assistant sees the whole conversation every time it answers. That is what makes follow-ups work.
A new chat starts with an empty page, so it would not know what "that" means. Staying in this chat is what keeps the context.
You do not need to repeat anything. The earlier conversation is already part of the context.
check.explain: Inside one chat, everything said so far is the context. That is why a short follow-up like "an example of that" works.

lessons.title: Tell it what to change
lessons.goal: You can steer an answer with specific feedback instead of starting again.
lessons.theory:
The first answer is a first draft. If it is not quite right, do not give up and do not start over. Tell the assistant what to change, the way you would with a friend who is helping you.

Good feedback is specific. Compare:

```text
no that's bad
```

```text
That's too long and uses words I don't know. Make it shorter, about 5 sentences, and use simpler words. Add one everyday example.
```

The second says **what was wrong** (too long, hard words) and **what you want instead** (shorter, simpler, an example).

Feedback phrases that work well:

- **Length:** "shorter", "in 3 sentences", "in more detail"
- **Level:** "simpler", "explain it like I'm new to this", "less basic, I know the basics"
- **Examples:** "give me two examples", "add a real-life comparison"
- **Style:** "as a bullet list", "friendlier", "more formal"

The assistant can see its earlier answer in the context, so you can point at it: "your second paragraph", "that example", "the list above".

You can give feedback as many times as you like, and each round gets you closer. Small, clear changes work better than "do it all again but better".
lessons.task: The assistant explained the water cycle, but the answer was long and full of hard words. Write a feedback message that says what was wrong and asks for a shorter, simpler version with at least one example.
lessons.hint: Say what was wrong first. Then ask for three changes: the length, simpler words and an example.
lessons.solution: That answer was too long and used a lot of hard words I didn't understand. Please make it shorter, about 5 sentences, and use simple everyday words. Add one example from real life, like a puddle drying up on a sunny day.

rubric.label: Says what was wrong with the answer
Asks for a shorter answer
Asks for simpler words
Asks for an example

check.explain: Your feedback names the problem and the fix: shorter, simpler, with an example. The assistant can see its earlier answer, so it knows exactly what to rewrite.
check.alternative: I got lost in all the technical terms. Could you redo it in three short sentences, explained like I'm new to science? Then give me an example of the water cycle I could see at home.
check.weak: Do it again but better please.

lessons.title: New topic, new chat
lessons.goal: You can decide when to keep going in the same chat and when to start a new one.
lessons.theory:
Follow-ups are great while you stay on one topic. But when you switch to something completely different, it is usually better to **start a new chat**.

Why? Everything in the chat is context, and the assistant tries to use it. If you spent twenty messages on a Spanish essay and then ask about a maths problem, bits of the old conversation can leak in. It might answer in Spanish, keep the same tone, or mix up the two tasks. Very long chats can also make it lose track of details.

Stay in the same chat when:

- you are asking follow-up questions about the same thing
- you are giving feedback on its last answer
- you are working on one project step by step

Start a new chat when:

- the topic changes completely
- the conversation has become very long and messy
- the answers keep going in the wrong direction and your corrections are not fixing it

A fresh chat gives you a clean context, answers focused only on the new question, and an easy way to find the conversation later, because each chat has one topic.

Starting over is not failure. It is often the quickest fix. If some details from the old chat still matter, copy them into your first message in the new one.
lessons.task: You have been chatting with an assistant for an hour about your short story. Now you want help understanding fractions for tomorrow's maths lesson. What is the best move?
lessons.hint: Is the new question about the same thing as the rest of the chat?

options: Stay in the story chat, so the assistant keeps your writing style in mind while it explains fractions.
Stay in the story chat, but write the fractions question in capital letters so it knows the topic changed.
Start a new chat for fractions, and go back to the story chat when you work on your story again.
Close the story chat for good, because you can only have one chat at a time.
why: Your story is no help with fractions. The old context can leak in and make the answer less focused.
Capital letters do not clear the context. The whole story conversation is still there for the assistant to use.
Right. A new topic gets a clean context, and the story chat stays ready for later.
You can have many chats. Keep the story one so you can pick it up again later.
check.explain: A completely new topic deserves a clean context. The fractions answer stays focused, and your story chat is still there when you need it.

lessons.title: Explain it like I'm a beginner
lessons.goal: You can ask for an explanation at your level, in simple words, with an everyday comparison.
lessons.theory:
An assistant can explain the same idea at many levels: for a young child, for a student your age, or for a university expert. If you do not say which level you want, it guesses, and it often guesses too high.

So tell it where you are starting from:

- **Your level:** "I'm a beginner", "I'm in year 8" (or "grade 8"), "I know what atoms are but not molecules"
- **The words you want:** "use simple words", "explain any technical words you use"
- **A comparison:** "compare it to something from everyday life"

Everyday comparisons, called **analogies**, are one of the best learning tools. Electricity in a wire is a bit like water in a pipe. A computer's memory is a bit like a desk: the bigger it is, the more you can work on at once. A good analogy gives the new idea something familiar to hang on.

Here is a strong beginner request:

```text
I'm new to economics. Can you explain what inflation is using simple words? Compare it to something from everyday life, like pocket money or prices at a shop.
```

You only need to share your level, not personal details. "I'm a beginner" or "I'm in year 9" is plenty. Your name and your school are never needed.

If the answer is still too hard, say so. If it is too easy, ask it to go one step deeper.
lessons.task: Pick any topic you want to understand better (for example how the internet works, black holes or how music is recorded). Write a prompt that asks for an explanation, says you are a beginner or gives your level, asks for simple words and asks for an everyday comparison.
lessons.hint: Check that your prompt has four things: what to explain, your level, simple words and a comparison to everyday life.
lessons.solution: I'm a beginner and I have never studied physics. Can you explain how black holes form, using simple words? Please compare it to something from everyday life so I can picture it.

rubric.label: Asks for an explanation
Says your level (a beginner, your year, or what you already know)
Asks for simple words
Asks for an everyday comparison

check.explain: Telling the assistant your level stops it guessing too high, simple words keep it readable, and an everyday comparison gives the new idea something familiar to attach to.
check.alternative: What is the internet and how does data get from one computer to another? I'm in year 7 and I don't know much about computers, so keep the language easy and use an analogy, like sending letters by post.
check.weak: Explain black holes.

lessons.title: Let it quiz you
lessons.goal: You can set up an AI quiz that asks one question at a time and gives feedback on every answer.
lessons.theory:
Reading an explanation feels like learning, but testing yourself is what makes it stick. An AI assistant makes a great quiz partner: it never gets bored, and it can explain every mistake.

The trick is to set the quiz up clearly. Otherwise the assistant may dump ten questions **and** all the answers in one go, which spoils it. A good quiz request says:

- **the topic** you are practising
- **how many questions**, and what kind (multiple choice, short answer, true or false)
- **one at a time**: ask it to wait for your answer before the next question
- **feedback**: tell you if you were right, and explain when you were wrong

```text
Quiz me on the causes of World War I. Ask me 5 short-answer questions, one at a time, and wait for my answer before asking the next one. After each answer, tell me if I was right and explain anything I got wrong.
```

At the end, you can ask "Which topics should I review?" or "Give me 3 harder questions on the parts I missed."

One caution from chapter 0: the assistant can make mistakes, even in its own quiz. If a question or a marking seems off, check your notes or textbook. Politely disagreeing ("I think it started in 1914, not 1916") is a good way to learn too.
lessons.task: Choose a subject you are studying or a hobby you love. Write a prompt that asks the assistant to quiz you: name the topic, say how many questions, ask for one question at a time, and ask for feedback on each answer.
lessons.hint: Four parts: the topic, a number of questions, one question at a time (wait for my answer), and feedback after each answer.
lessons.solution: Quiz me on the parts of a plant cell for my biology test. Ask me 6 multiple-choice questions, one at a time, and wait for my answer before the next one. After each answer, tell me if I was right and explain the correct answer if I was wrong.

rubric.label: Asks to be quizzed or tested
Says how many questions
Asks for one question at a time
Asks for feedback on your answers

check.explain: Your quiz has a topic, a clear size, one question at a time and feedback on each answer. That turns the assistant into a patient practice partner instead of an answer sheet.
check.alternative: I'm learning guitar chords. Can you test me with 5 questions about which notes are in each chord? Give me one question, then wait until I reply. Let me know whether I got it and give me feedback on my mistakes.
check.weak: Quiz me on plant cells.

lessons.title: The six parts of a prompt
lessons.goal: You can name the six parts of a strong prompt and spot whether a prompt has a clear task.
lessons.theory:
In chapter 1 you learned to ask one clear thing. Now you will learn to write **prompts**: messages to an AI assistant that are built on purpose to get exactly what you need.

A strong prompt can have up to six parts:

- **Role:** who the assistant should act as
- **Task:** what you want it to do
- **Context:** the background it needs
- **Constraints:** limits such as length, level and what to avoid
- **Format:** how the answer should be laid out
- **Examples:** a sample of what you want

Not every prompt needs all six. A quick question needs only a task. But the more the answer matters, the more the other parts help. In this chapter you add one part per mission.

The **task** is the heart of every prompt. A good task starts with a clear action word and names what you get back:

- "Explain how coral reefs form."
- "List five threats to coral reefs."
- "Suggest three titles for my talk about coral reefs."
- "Summarise this paragraph in two sentences."

Compare that with "coral reefs?" or "I have a presentation about coral reefs". Those give a topic but no task. The assistant has to guess whether you want facts, a plan, a script or a pep talk.

Rule of thumb: if you cannot point to the word that says what to do, the task is missing.
lessons.task: Which prompt has the clearest task?
lessons.hint: Find the option with an action word that says what the assistant should produce.

options: Coral reefs are really interesting and I have a presentation soon.
Suggest three catchy titles for a 5-minute class talk about coral reefs.
Coral reefs, school, presentation, science.
You are a marine biologist.
why: It gives background but never says what to do. Facts, a plan, a script? The assistant has to guess.
Right. A clear action word (suggest), what you get back (three titles) and the topic.
A list of keywords is a topic, not a task. No action word tells the assistant what to produce.
That is a role, which you add in the next mission. On its own it gives no task at all.
check.explain: It has a clear action word (suggest), says what you get back (three titles) and names the topic.

lessons.title: Give it a role
lessons.goal: You can open a prompt with a role that fits your task, followed by a clear task.
lessons.theory:
The **role** tells the assistant who to be while it answers. It usually goes in the first line of a prompt:

```text
You are a friendly science teacher.
```

Why does this help? The model learned from text written by many kinds of people: teachers, scientists, coaches, comedians. A role nudges it toward the knowledge, words and tone that fit that kind of person. A patient tutor explains and checks that you understand. A sports coach is direct and encouraging. A museum guide tells stories.

Common ways to write a role:

- "You are a patient maths tutor."
- "Act as an editor for a school newspaper."
- "Imagine you are a tour guide in ancient Rome."
- "Pretend to be a coach helping a beginner runner."

A role on its own does nothing. It needs a task after it:

```text
You are a marine biologist who loves teaching kids. Explain how coral reefs form.
```

Keep in mind that a role changes the style and focus, not the truth. Telling the assistant "you are a doctor" does not give it a medical degree, and its facts still need checking. Pick roles that help you learn: tutor, coach, editor, guide, quiz master.
lessons.task: Write a prompt that gives the assistant a role and then a clear task. Use any topic you like: a school subject, a hobby or a project.
lessons.hint: Start with a line such as "You are..." or "Act as...", then say what you want it to do.
lessons.solution: You are a friendly marine biologist who loves teaching students. Explain how coral reefs form and why they need warm, clear water.

rubric.label: Gives the assistant a role
Gives a task with an action word (explain, suggest, list...)

check.explain: Your role sets the tone and focus, and your task says exactly what to do. Together they already beat a bare question.
check.alternative: Act as a patient chess coach for a beginner. Suggest three simple opening moves and tell me the idea behind each one.
check.weak: Tell me about volcanoes.

lessons.title: Add context
lessons.goal: You can add context to a prompt: why you need the answer, who it is for and what you already know.
lessons.theory:
**Context** is the background the assistant needs to fit the answer to your situation. Without it, you get an answer written for everyone, which often means an answer that fits no one.

Useful context answers questions like:

- **Why do you need it?** "I'm giving a 5-minute talk on Friday."
- **Who is it for?** "This is for my class of 12-year-olds."
- **What do you already know or have?** "I already know what coral is. I have three photos of a reef."
- **What have you tried?** "My first draft felt boring."

Watch the difference:

```text
You are a science teacher. Explain coral bleaching.
```

```text
You are a science teacher. Explain coral bleaching. I'm preparing a 5-minute talk for my class, and I already know that coral is an animal, not a plant.
```

The second assistant knows the audience, the purpose and what to skip. Its answer will be shorter, more focused and more useful.

A good test: imagine handing your prompt to a helpful person who has never met you. What would they need to ask before starting? Put those answers in.

Only share what helps the task. Your level, your goal and your deadline are useful. Your full name, address, school name and passwords are never needed, and you will learn more about privacy later in the course.
lessons.task: The box holds a prompt with a role and a task. Add two pieces of context: why you need the answer (or who it is for), and what you already know. You can also write your own prompt on another topic, as long as it has a role, a task and both pieces of context.
lessons.hint: Keep the role and the task, then add a sentence like "I'm preparing..." or "This is for..." and one like "I already know...".
lessons.starter: You are a science teacher. Explain how coral reefs form.
lessons.solution: You are a science teacher. Explain how coral reefs form. I'm preparing a 5-minute talk for my class on Friday, and I already know that coral is a tiny animal, so you can skip that part.

rubric.label: Gives the assistant a role
Gives a task with an action word
Says why you need it or who it is for
Says what you already know or have

check.explain: Now the assistant knows your purpose and your starting point, so it can skip what you know and aim at what you need.
check.alternative: Act as an experienced baking coach. Suggest a simple cake I can bake for my grandmother's birthday this weekend. I have made cookies before but never a cake, and I only have one round tin.
check.weak: You are a teacher. Explain volcanoes.

lessons.title: Set the limits
lessons.goal: You can add constraints to a prompt: a length limit, a level, and something to avoid.
lessons.theory:
**Constraints** are the limits and rules the answer must follow. They stop the assistant from writing too much, aiming at the wrong level or including things you do not want.

Three kinds of constraint do most of the work:

- **Length:** "under 150 words", "in 3 bullet points", "one short paragraph"
- **Level:** "for a 12-year-old", "for a beginner", "at the level of year 9 science"
- **What to avoid:** "don't use technical words", "avoid long quotes", "don't give me the final answer, just hints"

That last one is great for learning. When you are stuck on a maths problem, ask for a hint instead of the solution, so you still do the thinking.

Constraints go after the task and context:

```text
You are a science teacher. Explain how coral reefs form. I'm preparing a 5-minute talk for my class. Keep it under 150 words, write it for 12-year-olds, and don't use any Latin names.
```

Be precise. "Short" means different things to different people; "under 100 words" means one thing. And say what you **do** want as well as what to avoid, so the assistant has somewhere to go.

Models are not perfect at exact counts, so "150 words" may come out as 140 or 170. That is fine. If it is way off, give feedback and ask again.
lessons.task: Write a prompt with a task and three constraints: a length limit, a level, and one thing to avoid. You can add a role and context too. One idea: ask for hints on a tricky maths problem without being given the final answer.
lessons.hint: After your task, add three limits: how long (a number of words or sentences), who it is for, and something it should not do.
lessons.solution: You are a patient maths tutor. Help me solve 3x + 7 = 22 by giving me hints one step at a time. Write for a year 8 student, keep each hint under 30 words, and don't tell me the final answer until I ask for it.

Says what to avoid

check.alternative: Explain how a bicycle's gears make pedalling easier on hills. I'm a beginner with no physics background. Keep it to one short paragraph and avoid equations.
check.weak: Explain how gears work on a bike. Make it good.

lessons.title: Choose the format
lessons.goal: You can pick the layout that fits what you will do with the answer: a list, steps, a table, flashcards or an outline.
lessons.theory:
The **format** is how the answer is laid out. The same information can come as a wall of text or as something you can use straight away. If you do not ask, the assistant picks for you.

Formats worth knowing:

- **Bullet list:** quick points, easy to scan
- **Numbered steps:** instructions in order, like a recipe
- **Table:** comparing things side by side, with columns you name
- **Headings and short sections:** longer notes or a study guide
- **Question and answer pairs:** flashcards for revision
- **Outline:** the skeleton of an essay or a talk, before you write it yourself

Say the format plainly, and add the details:

```text
Compare Mars and Venus in a table with three columns: feature, Mars, Venus. Include size, temperature and length of a day.
```

```text
Turn my notes below into 10 flashcards. Write each one as Q: on one line and A: on the next.
```

Choose the format by what you will **do** with the answer. Revising? Flashcards. Comparing? A table. Following a process? Numbered steps. Planning your own essay? An outline, so the writing stays yours.

You can also change the format later with feedback: "Now put that in a table."
lessons.task: You want to compare three musical instruments (guitar, piano and violin) on price, how hard they are to learn and how easy they are to carry. Which request gives you the most useful layout?
lessons.hint: Which layout lets you see all three instruments side by side?

options: Tell me about guitar, piano and violin.
Write me a long essay about which instrument is best.
Describe each instrument in its own paragraph, one after another.
Make a table with one row per instrument and columns for price, difficulty to learn and how easy it is to carry.
why: No format at all. You will probably get long paragraphs and have to dig out the comparison yourself.
An essay is hard to scan, and you did not ask for a winner. You wanted three features side by side.
Separate paragraphs make you jump back and forth to compare. Side-by-side comparison is what tables are for.
Right. A table puts every instrument and every feature in one view, and naming the columns makes sure nothing is missed.
check.explain: Comparing several things on the same features is exactly what a table is for, and naming the columns makes sure every feature is covered.

lessons.title: Show an example
lessons.goal: You can put an example in a prompt so the assistant copies the style and shape you want.
lessons.theory:
Sometimes it is hard to describe exactly what you want. Then the easiest move is to **show** it. Put an example in your prompt, and the assistant will follow its style, length and shape.

This works because the model is a pattern-matcher. One or two examples tell it more than a paragraph of description.

```text
Write 5 more revision questions about the water cycle in the same style as these:

Q: What is it called when water vapour turns into liquid?
A: Condensation.

Q: What is it called when water falls from clouds?
A: Precipitation.
```

Now the assistant knows: a short question, a one-word answer, the Q: and A: labels, and the level of difficulty.

Examples are great for:

- **Style:** "Write a riddle about a planet, like this one: ..."
- **Tone:** paste a paragraph you wrote and say "match my voice"
- **Structure:** show one finished item of a list and ask for more like it

Tips:

- Say clearly that it is an example: "like this", "in the same style as", "for example".
- Use good examples, because it will copy the flaws too.
- With only one example, it may copy it too closely. Two or three different ones help it see the pattern, not just the words.
lessons.task: You want 10 fun facts about sharks for a club poster, each one short and numbered, like "1. Sharks have been around longer than trees." What is the best way to get exactly that style?
lessons.hint: The model is very good at copying a pattern it can see.

options: Put one or two facts in your prompt, written exactly the way you want the rest, and say "in the same style as these".
Just ask for "shark facts" and hope the style comes out right.
Describe the style in a long paragraph, but never show an actual fact.
Ask for 100 facts, so that at least a few come out in the right style.
why: Right. Real examples show the length, the numbering and the tone at a glance, and the model follows the pattern.
Without an example or a format, the assistant picks its own style, which may be long paragraphs.
A description can help, but showing one or two real examples is quicker and clearer. The model copies patterns it can see.
More output does not fix the style. You would get a pile of text to sort through, all in whatever style it guessed.
check.explain: An example shows the style, the length and the numbering all at once. The model is a pattern-matcher, so it follows what it can see.

lessons.title: The full prompt
lessons.goal: You can write one prompt that has all six parts: role, task, context, constraints, format and an example.
lessons.theory:
You now know all six parts. Time to put them together.

Here is a full prompt with each part on its own line, so you can spot them:

```text
You are an enthusiastic geography teacher.
Help me plan a 5-minute class presentation about coral reefs.
I'm in year 8, I've read one article about reefs, and my classmates know very little about them.
Keep it simple enough for 12-year-olds, and don't include any statistics, because I will add checked ones myself.
Give me an outline with 4 sections, each with a heading and 2 or 3 bullet points.
For example: "1. What is a reef? - A reef is built by tiny animals called polyps."
```

Line by line: role, task, context, constraints, format, example.

Notice what this prompt does **not** ask for: a finished script. The outline gives the structure, and you write and say the words yourself. That is how you learn, and how you stay the author of your own work.

For a quick question, a clear task is enough. For anything that matters, like a project or a study plan, the full recipe pays off.

Before you press enter, check:

- Did I say who it should be?
- Is the task one clear action?
- Does it know my situation?
- Did I set limits on length, level or what to avoid?
- Did I say how to lay it out?
- Would an example make it clearer?
lessons.task: Write a complete prompt for a school project or a hobby of your choice. It must have all six parts: a role, a task, context, constraints, a format and an example.
lessons.hint: Go down the checklist at the end of the briefing and make sure your prompt answers every question, with a sentence or two per part.
lessons.solution: You are a friendly and experienced running coach. Make me a 4-week plan to go from walking to running 3 km without stopping. I'm a beginner, I play football once a week, and right now I can jog for about 5 minutes. Keep each session under 30 minutes and don't include anything that needs a gym. Put it in a table with columns for week, day and what to do. For example: Week 1 | Monday | Walk 5 min, jog 1 min, repeat 4 times.

Sets constraints: length, level or what to avoid

Includes an example of what you want

Please use simple language and avoid long paragraphs. Give me 8 flashcards with a question on one line and the answer on the next, such as Q: Whose improved steam engine was patented in 1769? A: James Watt.

lessons.title: Think step by step
lessons.goal: You can explain why asking for step-by-step working helps, and how to use it to learn a method.
lessons.theory:
Some questions cannot be answered in one leap: a maths word problem, a logic puzzle, planning a week of revision. For these, ask the assistant to **work through it step by step**.

```text
A train leaves at 9:40 and the trip takes 2 hours 35 minutes. What time does it arrive? Work through it step by step.
```

Why does this help? The assistant writes its answer one piece at a time. When it writes out each step, every later step can build on the earlier ones, right there in front of it. When it jumps straight to the answer, there is no working to lean on, and slips are more likely.

Many newer assistants already reason quietly before they reply, especially on hard problems. Asking for the steps is still worth it, for another reason: **you can check them**. If step 3 is wrong, you can see it and say so. And seeing the steps is how you learn the method, not just the result.

Even better for learning:

- "Show me only the first step, then let me try the next one."
- "Give me a hint for the next step instead of the answer."
- "Check my working and tell me where I went wrong."

A tidy chain of steps can still contain an error, so read it the way a teacher would: one step at a time.
lessons.task: Why is it useful to ask an assistant to solve a tricky maths problem step by step?
lessons.hint: Think about what the written steps do for the assistant, and what they let you do.

options: It makes the answer longer, and longer answers are always correct.
It makes the assistant look the answer up on the internet.
Each step can build on the steps written before it, and you can check the working and learn the method.
It guarantees there are no mistakes, so you never need to check.
why: Length is not accuracy. The benefit is that each step builds on the last, and you can check them.
Step-by-step working has nothing to do with web search. It changes how the assistant writes the answer, not where the information comes from.
Right. Written steps give each new step something to build on, and they let you spot errors and learn how it is done.
No method guarantees a correct answer. A chain of steps can still hide an error, which is exactly why you read it.
check.explain: Written steps give each later step something to build on, and they let you check the working and learn the method yourself.

lessons.title: Ask for options, then compare
lessons.goal: You can ask for several different options and a comparison, then make the choice yourself.
lessons.theory:
When there is no single right answer, like a title, a project idea or a way to start a story, do not settle for the first thing the assistant says. **Ask for several options** and compare them.

```text
Give me 4 different ideas for a science fair project about sound, using things I can find at home. For each one, give one advantage and one disadvantage. Then tell me which you would pick for a beginner and why.
```

This prompt does three things:

- asks for a **number** of options (4)
- asks for them to be **different**, so you do not get four versions of the same idea
- asks for a **comparison**: pros and cons, and a recommendation with a reason

Why it works: the first idea is only one possibility. Seeing several side by side helps you notice what you actually like. Often the best result is a mix: "Take the title from option 2 and the experiment from option 4."

You stay the decision-maker. The assistant's recommendation is one opinion, based only on what you told it. You know your time, your materials and what excites you.

This works for titles, essay angles, ways to explain an idea, band names, study plans and much more. Whenever you catch yourself accepting the first answer to a creative question, ask for three more.
lessons.task: Write a prompt that asks for several different options for something creative (a project idea, a title, a club name, a story opening...) and asks the assistant to compare them.
lessons.hint: Say how many options you want, ask for them to be different, and ask for pros and cons or a recommendation.
lessons.solution: Give me 5 different titles for my short story about a girl who finds a map inside a library book. Make them varied: some mysterious, some funny. For each one, say what mood it sets, then compare them and tell me which fits a mystery story best and why.

rubric.label: Asks for several options
Asks for them to be different from each other
Asks for a comparison (pros and cons, or which is best)

check.explain: You asked for a spread of different options and a comparison, so you can see the choices side by side and pick or mix the best parts yourself.
check.alternative: I'm starting a chess club at school and need a name. Can you suggest a few options that are quite different from each other? Then list the pros and cons of each so I can choose.
check.weak: Give me a name for my chess club.

lessons.title: Ask it to check its own work
lessons.goal: You can ask the assistant to review its answer against clear criteria, list the problems and write a better version.
lessons.theory:
An assistant's first answer is a first draft. You can often get a better one by asking it to **review its own answer** and improve it.

```text
Now check your answer. Does it follow everything I asked for? List any problems, like missing parts, mistakes or unclear sentences. Then write an improved version.
```

Why does this work? While writing the first answer, it was moving forward word by word. When you ask for a review, the whole answer is already in the context, so it can look at it as a whole and compare it with your request. It is a bit like re-reading your own essay the next day.

To make the review useful, give it something to check against:

- **Your requirements:** "Is it under 150 words, with no jargon?"
- **A quality list:** "Is it clear, correct and in a sensible order?"
- **A reader:** "Would a 12-year-old understand every sentence?"

Then ask for two things: a list of the problems **and** a new version. Seeing the problems teaches you what to look for next time.

A warning: self-review helps, but it is not proof. The assistant can miss its own mistakes, or "fix" something that was right. You are still the final checker, especially for facts.

The same trick works on your own work: paste a paragraph you wrote and ask for feedback, not a rewrite, so the writing stays yours.
lessons.task: The assistant just wrote you a short explanation of how vaccines work, for a class poster. Write a follow-up message that asks it to review its answer against clear criteria, list the problems it finds, and then write an improved version.
lessons.hint: Ask for a review, name what to check (for example: correct, clear, a word limit), ask for a list of problems, then ask for a better version.
lessons.solution: Please review your explanation. Check that it is correct, clear enough for 12-year-olds and under 100 words. List any problems you find, like hard words or missing steps, then write an improved version that fixes them.

rubric.label: Asks it to review or check its answer
Gives criteria to check against (correct, clear, a length, a reader...)
Asks for a list of the problems
Asks for an improved version

check.explain: You gave the review a target, asked to see the problems and asked for a fix. You get a better answer and learn what to look for yourself.
check.alternative: Read over what you wrote as if you were a strict science teacher. Is anything inaccurate or too technical for a poster? Point out the weak spots and then give me a better version.
check.weak: Is that right?

lessons.title: Small steps win
lessons.goal: You can build a big result in small steps, changing one thing at a time and saying what to keep.
lessons.theory:
Big tasks go wrong in big ways. Ask for a whole study plan, a whole story or a whole project in one prompt, and you get a long answer that is hard to fix. Change one thing and something else breaks.

The better way is to **iterate in small steps**: build the result piece by piece, and check each piece before moving on.

For example, planning a short film for your media club:

- First: "Suggest 5 ideas for a 3-minute film we can shoot at school." Pick one.
- Then: "Write a one-paragraph outline of idea 2." Adjust it.
- Then: "Break the outline into 6 scenes." Fix the order.
- Then: "For scene 1, suggest camera shots we can do with a phone."

At each step you look, decide and steer. Mistakes stay small and easy to catch. And you stay in charge of the project, instead of accepting a big block of text you did not shape.

Two habits make this work:

- **Change one thing at a time.** Ask for five changes at once and it is hard to tell what helped. "Make scene 3 funnier" is easier to judge than "make everything better".
- **Say what to keep.** "Keep the ending, but change the opening." Otherwise the assistant may rewrite parts you liked.

When a chat gets long and messy, sum up what you have decided so far and carry it into a new chat.
lessons.task: You asked for a plan for a school garden and got a long plan. You like most of it, but the plant list is wrong for your climate. What is the best next message?
lessons.hint: Look for the message that changes one thing and protects the rest.

options: Start again with "Write a better garden plan."
Rewrite the whole plan: change the plants, the layout, the schedule and the budget, and make it more fun.
That's not right.
Keep everything else the same, but replace the plant list with plants that grow well in a cool, rainy climate.
why: Starting over throws away the parts you liked, and "better" does not say what was wrong.
Five changes at once make it hard to see what improved, and it will rewrite parts you already liked.
It says something is wrong, but not what or how to fix it. The assistant has to guess.
Right. One clear change, and you told it what to keep.
check.explain: It changes one thing, says exactly what, and tells the assistant what to keep. Small, clear steps keep the good parts safe.

lessons.title: Let it ask you first
lessons.goal: You can ask the assistant to interview you with a few questions before it answers.
lessons.theory:
Sometimes you do not know which details the assistant needs, for example when you want help with something new, like starting a hobby or planning a project. Then flip the conversation around: **ask the assistant to ask you questions first**.

```text
I want to start learning to draw. Before you give me any advice, ask me up to 5 questions about what I need, one at a time. Wait for my answers, then suggest a plan.
```

This works well because the assistant has seen many conversations about learning and planning, so it often knows which details matter: your level, your time, your materials, your goal. It turns that into questions, and your answers become the context for a much better plan.

Three details make it work:

- **Questions first, answer later.** Say it clearly, or it may ask one question and then carry on with a full answer anyway.
- **Set a limit**, like 3 to 5 questions, so it does not interview you forever.
- **Say what comes after:** the plan, the advice or the draft you actually want.

You can also say: "Keep asking until you have what you need, but no more than 5 questions."

As always, answer with what helps the task. Your level, your goals and your free time are useful. Private details like your address or passwords never are.

lessons.solution: I want to start learning to play the ukulele. Before you give me any advice, ask me up to 5 questions about my goals, my free time and what I already know, one at a time. Wait for my answers, then suggest a 4-week practice plan.

lessons.title: Your reusable prompt template
lessons.goal: You can turn a prompt that works into a reusable template with named blanks.
lessons.theory:
When a prompt works really well, do not lose it. Save it as a **template**: a prompt with blanks that you fill in each time.

```text
You are a patient tutor for [SUBJECT].
I'm studying [TOPIC] for [WHY: a test, a project...].
I already know [WHAT I KNOW], but I'm confused about [WHAT IS HARD].
Explain it in simple words, in under [NUMBER] words, with one everyday example.
Then quiz me with [NUMBER] questions, one at a time, and wait for my answer each time.
```

Next week, for a different subject, you only fill in the blanks. You get a strong prompt in seconds, and it always includes the parts you learned in this course.

Good templates:

- Put blanks in **[SQUARE BRACKETS]** with capital letters, so you cannot miss one.
- Name each blank clearly: [TOPIC] is better than [X].
- Keep the parts that always help: role, constraints, format.
- Build in tricks from this chapter: step by step, options, self-review, questions first.

Where do you keep them? A notes app or a document works fine. Many assistants also let you save instructions or prompts inside the app itself. The names and buttons change often, so look in your assistant's settings or help pages. You will see more about this later in the course.

Start small: one template for studying, one for feedback on your writing, one for planning projects. Improve them each time you use them.
